ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Consider a metallic sphere of radius $R$, attached to the ground (zero potential), and a point charge $q$ located at a distance $L$ from the center of the sphere. We will use the method of images to solve this electrostatics problem. Assume metals are excellent conductors and polarize much faster than the system's relaxation time.

1. Place an image charge inside the sphere to counter the non-uniform potential of the outer charge $q$ on the surface. Determine the location and value of this image charge.
2. Find the force of attraction between the charge and the sphere. 
(Note: There are no mathematical expressions in the provided text to convert to LaTeX format.)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Consider a metallic sphere of radius $R$, attached to the ground (zero potential), and a point charge $q$ located at a distance $L$ from the center of the sphere. Use the method of images to solve this electrostatics problem. Assume metals are excellent conductors and polarize much faster than the system's relaxation time. 1. Place an image charge inside the sphere to counter the non-uniform potential of the outer charge $q$ on the surface. Determine the location and value of this image charge. 2. Find the force of attraction between the charge and the sphere.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Set the sphere center as the origin, and place the real point charge q on the z-axis at z = L, with L > R. Assume one image charge q0 on the same axis at z = x inside the grounded sphere. For a point on the sphere surface at polar angle theta, the distance to the real charge is r_q = sqrt(R^2 + L^2 - 2 R L cos(theta)), and the distance to the image charge is r_0 = sqrt(R^2 + x^2 - 2 R x cos(theta)). The boundary condition for a grounded conducting sphere is V(R,theta) = k(q/r_q + q0/r_0) = 0 for every theta, where k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0). To make this cancellation possible for all theta, choose x so that r_0 is a constant multiple of r_q. Matching the quadratic forms gives x = R^2/L. Then r_0^2 = (R^2/L^2) r_q^2, so r_0 = (R/L) r_q. Substituting into the boundary condition gives k/r_q [q + q0(L/R)] = 0, hence q0 = -q R/L. The force on the real charge is equal to the Coulomb force exerted by the image charge. Their separation is L - x = L - R^2/L. Since q0 has the opposite sign to q, the force is attractive and points from the charge toward the sphere. Its magnitude is F = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) q^2 (R/L)/(L - R^2/L)^2.
